title: The Evening Brief: Senate blocks crypto clarity bill; Circle launches Arc mainnet tomorrow
dek: The Senate's 49-50 vote against the Digital Asset Market Clarity Act on September 15 ended a year of bipartisan negotiation over ethics provisions, while institutional settlement infrastructure moves ahead: Circle's Arc blockchain launches September 16 with BlackRock, DTCC, Visa, and Mastercard as founding validators. The market's mood is neutral and prices are flat.
author: Crypto Cronkite
key_fact: Federal crypto regulation stalled on ethics disagreement between parties, but institutional adoption, tokenized bonds in India, validators from Wall Street, and compliance-driven stablecoins, is advancing on its own calendar independent of Congress.
bottom_line: Security incidents, the Revolut breach, the Symbiosis bridge exploit, the Robinhood insider-trading charges, underscore that adoption speed has outpaced maturity in both custody and DeFi. Watch the September 16 House Ways and Means markup on the tax bill, the Balancer Snapshot vote September 25-29, and whether Arc's founding validators actually accumulate settlement volume before the ARC token's May 2028 delivery deadline.
body: The U.S. Senate rejected the Digital Asset Market Clarity Act on September 15 in a 49-50 procedural vote, blocking floor debate on the first comprehensive federal crypto market structure bill after a year of bipartisan negotiations. Four Senate Republicans (Susan Collins, Josh Hawley, Jerry Moran, Thom Tillis) joined all 50 Democratic votes to oppose a cloture motion required under an August 8 unanimous consent agreement. The sticking point was ethics provisions: seven Democrats who spent months shaping the bill, Kirsten Gillibrand, Mark Warner, Cory Booker, Raphael Warnock, Ruben Gallego, Angela Alsobrooks, Catherine Cortez Masto, voted no, citing language they said was too weak to prevent sitting officials from profiting off crypto ventures while overseeing crypto regulation. The House had passed H.R. 3633 by 294-134 in July 2025. Unless Senator Tillis forces a second cloture vote before the state work period closes on October 5, the Clarity Act is dead unless a new Congress revives it in 2027.

Institutional settlement infrastructure, by contrast, is moving ahead without waiting for Congress. Circle's Arc mainnet launches on September 16 with 11 named founding validators from Wall Street and payments: BlackRock, DTCC, Visa, Mastercard, ICE, and six others. Arc uses permissioned Proof-of-Authority consensus, a rotating validator proposes a block, more than two-thirds must pre-commit, and finalization is irreversible at the consensus layer, while keeping the application layer permissionless. The architecture separates validator control from application liability: neither Arc Network Services LLC nor the validators bear responsibility for third-party application content or legality. The presale structure requires the ARC token to be delivered or the network to transition to Proof-of-Stake by May 2028, a deadline that will test whether institutional participation can hold steady. Individual validator voting weights remain undisclosed at launch.

India's tokenized settlement infrastructure is already live. India's RBI and SEBI announced Demat 2.0 on September 10, and three companies completed tokenized bond offerings on September 7 and 9: REC Limited issued ₹500 crore, L&T Limited issued ₹500 crore, and IIFL issued ₹25 crore, moving ₹1,025 crore through the system. Each bond is a native digital token on a permissioned distributed ledger operated by India's depositories. Payment uses the wholesale digital rupee, the central bank's own currency. The two legs, bond and payment, settle atomically: either both complete or neither does, eliminating settlement risk. Retail participation and secondary-market trading are deferred to a later stage.

On the security front, the Revolut breach exposed cracks in metadata defenses. An attacker impersonating a government agency used a spoofed legitimate government domain to bypass Revolut's information-request controls and extracted personal identity documents, account statements, IBANs, and transaction records including Bitcoin activity from a "very limited" number of customers. The attacker is demanding 10,000 BTC (roughly $780 million) and threatening daily releases. Revolut has not authenticated the leaked material or confirmed the ransom demand, leaving the threat's legitimacy unclear. But the exposure of passports and crypto transaction histories creates immediate identity-theft risk for affected customers. Former Mt. Gox CEO Mark Karpelès was among those affected. On-chain investigator ZachXBT suggested the attackers may have specifically targeted wealthy users, and crypto analyst Max Karpis noted that a $780 million Bitcoin payment would be easily traced, making it extremely difficult for attackers to cash out.

Two Robinhood engineers face DOJ charges for alleged insider trading on decentralized derivatives. Hefu Chai, 36, and Huaisong Xiang, 30, were charged with wire fraud and commodities fraud for allegedly trading perpetual futures on Hyperliquid using nonpublic information about cryptocurrency listings Robinhood was preparing to announce between 2025 and 2026. Each defendant allegedly earned more than $50,000 from the trades. The charges represent allegations by prosecutors, not a court judgment; the procedural status and next hearing dates are not reported.

The Symbiosis bridge exploit illustrates the scale of vulnerability in cross-chain systems. Two software bugs allowed an attacker to create 46.1 billion syBTC tokens from a 330-satoshi deposit worth about 25 cents. The first bug caused the bridge to read the wrong part of a bitcoin transaction, allowing the attacker to be treated as both a depositor and administrator. The second bug permitted negative fees, which flipped the math: instead of reducing a deposit, subtraction added to it. The attacker processed 12 bogus deposits in four minutes across BNB Chain, Ethereum, and Rootstock. Symbiosis recovered 15 Bitcoin and offered a 20% bounty for further recovery after the attacker refused an initial white-hat bounty. Preliminary estimated losses are 9.97 BTC, approximately $770,000, but the protocol is offline through rewrite and independent audit.

Balancer is proposing a shutdown. The protocol's governance forum posted a shutdown proposal on September 15 to wind down operations and distribute its approximately $9 million treasury to BAL token holders through staged redemptions from May 2027 to July 2028. Monthly protocol revenue stood at $30,000 in August, down from $97,000 in June, against monthly burn of approximately $150,000. The April restructuring, BIP-918, had cut the operating budget 34% to $1.9 million, reduced staff from roughly 25 to 12.5, and set a review trigger if revenue fell below $60,000 monthly for three consecutive months. That threshold was crossed. The Snapshot vote on September 25-29 will decide whether Balancer enters its phase-out. If approved, the first redemption window opens May 31, 2027.

House Ways and Means released a 114-page crypto tax bill ahead of Thursday's committee markup. The Digital Asset Tax Certainty Act, filed as H.R. 10357, proposes a $10 exemption for blockchain network and transaction fees below that threshold that would not trigger a taxable event, though this exemption does not apply to users who executed more than 5,000 transfers in the prior year, limiting relief to retail participants. The committee markup is scheduled for September 16. The bill faces timeline pressure before November elections, and its survival depends on committee passage followed by subsequent floor time, both uncertain given the compressed House workload and political calendar.

CoinEx, a Hong Kong-based crypto exchange operating for nine years, will cease operations in December. Founder and CEO Haipo Yang cited falling trading volumes, liquidity constraints, prolonged crypto downturn, and rising compliance costs. The December closure deadline will require users to withdraw funds by that date.
